newsitem.title: FRANCE: Balladur bond bonanza seen bound for bourse.
newsitem.headline: Balladur bond bonanza seen bound for bourse.

text.p: The French stock market will grab the lion's share of some 91 billion francs which the French government is due to return to investors on July 16 when the so-called Balladur bond expires, analysts said on Monday.

Talk of a cash injection from the bond has already helped push the French CAC-40 index of leading shares up more than 16 percent in less than a month from 2,498.75 on June 2 to a record high of 2,903.18 on June 27, they said.

The second most likely beneficiary would be fixed income unit trusts, followed by life assurance contracts, although fears that life assurance assets could be targeted by the new Socialist government for heavier taxes is making many cautious.

"The (French) equity market is extremely sensitive to this liquidity wave coming from the Balladur bond -- people are buying even before it has been repaid," Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley, said.
The bond was issued in June 1993 to help finance an economic recovery programme launched by then conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur and it raised a hefty 110 billion francs.

Since then some of the bonds have been used to buy shares in privatised companies -- Elf, Rhone-Poulenc, Banque Nationale de Paris, Union des Assurances de Paris and Assurances Generales de France, for example.
Last year the Treasury repaid a lump sum cutting the amount of bonds outstanding to 90.88 billion francs.

The main reason that Balladur bond receipts are likely to be pumped back into equities is that nearly half of the bonds are in equity savings plans which are exempt from income and capital gains tax as long as the plan is kept intact for five years.
Figures from the Bank of France show that in March this year 35.23 billion francs of the Balladur bond was still in such plans, so-called "Plans d'Epargne en Actions" (PEAs).
The Balladur bond was eligible for PEAs because it was expected that many investors would convert them into shares of state-owned companies being privatised.
Traditionally holders of Balladur bonds had preferential access to shares in newly privatised companies.

PEAs were first launched on September 14, 1992. So if a plan had been set up before the bond was launched, and the bonds then bought by switching money within the fund, investors would have to keep the money in the PEA until September this year.

Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris, said it's "more or less a mystery" exactly where the rest of the bonds are being held, although he estimates that at least another 15 billion is in other kinds of equity unit trusts.
If correct, this would still leave another 40 billion francs in fixed interest funds.
Several bankers on origination desks in Paris say some French banks with a wide retail distribution network are getting ready to offer bonds for their own accounts to mop up the Balladur liquidity.

Credit Agricole captured the largest segment of the Balladur bond business in 1993. More than 300,000 of the bank's customers put 19.6 billion francs into the scheme. Societe Generale had 130,000 subscribers putting up a total of 12.3 billion francs.
At six percent, the coupon on the Balladur bond now looks relatively attractive compared with French 10-year government bonds yielding 5.58 percent.

Analysts said while this could prompt some investors to push money into the long-end of the yield curve, using life assurance contracts as a tax-efficient savings vehicle, the money could be parked in money-market funds until it becomes clear whether life assurance assets will be subject to new taxes.
"People are very nervous about life assurance at the moment," Chaney said.

He also said any Balladur money earmarked for the partial privatisation of France Telecom, which may well still take place later this year despite the change in government, could also be left in money-market funds for now.
Mange said the new government might have missed a chance in that the Balladur bond would have provided an immediate source of funds for a France Telecom sale.

However, he said it was ironic that by delaying any offer until after the French stock market had been pumped up with the Balladur bond money anyway, the government could reap the benefit of a higher valuation for France Telecom.
